blocks.title: A pipeline describes a transformation
paragraphs: A functional interface gives a lambda its parameter and result contract. A stream connects a source to intermediate transformations and a terminal operation. Reason about the values at each stage before compressing the code.

blocks.title: A lambda still has a type
paragraphs: Predicate<T> returns a boolean through test; Function<T,R> maps a T to R through apply; Supplier<T> provides a T through get. A lambda needs a compatible target functional interface. var alone cannot supply the missing type of an untyped lambda.
The callback below keeps no changing external state. It maps a reading to twice its value, then tests the mapped result. State-free callbacks make a transformation easier to reason about and test.

blocks.title: Trace filter, map, order and collection
paragraphs: For [6, 1, 4, 3], filtering values ≥3 leaves [6,4,3]; doubling gives [12,8,6]; sorting gives [6,8,12]. toList is the terminal operation that produces the result. Changing the order of filter and map can change which elements survive.

Intermediate stages are lazy: constructing the pipeline does not itself traverse all values. A terminal operation drives the needed traversal. Streams are single-use; create a fresh stream for a second query. For numeric reduction, mapToInt(...).sum() can produce a total; it is not another intermediate stream.
These examples use a sequential ordered list source. Do not infer guarantees about arbitrary sources, parallel execution or callback scheduling. No parallel-stream analysis is required here.

blocks.title: Absence is a result to handle
paragraphs: findFirst may return no matching value. Optional represents presence or absence without pretending that an arbitrary sentinel is a valid domain value. map transforms only a present value; orElse supplies a fallback when absent.

Calling get without checking presence can fail. Optional.of requires a non-null value; ofNullable can represent a possibly null source. Choose a fallback that is appropriate for the result type and requirements rather than hiding missing required data.

blocks.title: Follow values and finish the pipeline
paragraphs: Choose the functional type, trace each stage in order, name the terminal operation and handle absence explicitly. A compact pipeline is useful only when its semantics remain clear.

cards.prompt: Which functional interface fits a callback that accepts a value and answers yes/no?
cards.answer: Predicate<T>, whose test method returns boolean. Function<T,R> instead transforms a value; Supplier<T> takes no argument and provides a value.

cards.prompt: Why prefer callbacks that do not update external mutable state?
cards.answer: Their results are easier to reason about from inputs, repeated tests are clearer, and pipeline logic does not depend on hidden mutation or callback timing.

cards.prompt: Does list.stream().filter(predicate) by itself calculate the final filtered list?
cards.answer: No. It builds an intermediate lazy stage. A terminal operation such as toList, count or sum drives the required traversal.

cards.prompt: Can a consumed stream be traversed again for a second result?
cards.answer: No. Obtain a new stream from the source for another query. Keep the reusable collection if multiple traversals are needed.

cards.prompt: What happens to optional.map(f) when optional is empty?
cards.answer: It stays empty; f is not applied to a value. A terminal handling step such as orElse can then provide an explicit fallback.

cards.prompt: Does Optional.of(null) mean an empty Optional?
cards.answer: No. It rejects null. Optional.empty() explicitly represents absence, and Optional.ofNullable(value) handles a potentially null source.

guided.title: Describe a pipeline before coding
guided.prompt: A list of sensor durations may contain zero. Keep strictly positive durations, convert seconds to milliseconds, sort ascending and return a list. Separately request the first duration above 9 seconds, returning an explicit absent result if none exists.
rubric: The main pipeline preserves only positive values, converts units once and sorts the transformed values.
The search uses an Optional-like absent result without inventing a matching duration.
No side effects or unsupported ordering assumptions are required.
reference: The main output is [2000,4000,12000]. Predicate<Integer> fits filtering; Function<Integer,Integer> fits the conversion; toList finishes the pipeline.
For the separate search, filtering values >9 then findFirst returns 12 on this ordered source. An empty list or [4,0,2] yields an empty Optional. Build a fresh stream for each query.
